title: Inside the Pentagon, the pressure is on to find a home for a new spaceport
gist: The US Space Force wants a third heavy and super-heavy launch site by 2030 to relieve Cape Canaveral and Vandenberg, but Space Systems Command head Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant says there is no site, land plan or decision timeline yet. Florida and California hosted 175 orbital launch attempts last year and the Space Force projects 700 a year by 2036; options include a new federal installation, state land, public-private partnership or leasing commercial land such as SpaceX's planned Louisiana spaceport.

insights.claim: Space Force leaders want a third heavy-lift launch site running by 2030 to relieve Florida and California bases that have launched rockets for nearly 70 years, but the Pentagon has not chosen a location or decided how to acquire land.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A new federal launch-infrastructure program could create construction and launch-services opportunities, but the timing is highly uncertain.
insights.locator: Leaders in the US Space Force

insights.claim: Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said in May that a congressionally mandated study of launch infrastructure found the need for another site capable of heavy and super-heavy launches.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The site has congressional backing through the study requirement.
insights.quote: another site that’s capable of heavy and super heavy launch capability

insights.claim: Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command, called 2030 a need but said building a spaceport is a non-trivial demand given orbital regimes, safety, commodity access and neighbors, and that there are no decision timelines yet.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The official tone suggests the 2030 target is likely to slip.
insights.quote: We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist

insights.claim: The Trump administration's August space transportation policy endorsed building more launch and reentry sites for commercial and military missions.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.locator: The Trump administration released a space transportation policy

insights.claim: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Kennedy Space Center and Vandenberg Space Force Base hosted 175 orbital launch attempts last year, and the Space Force projects US spaceports will need to support 700 launches a year by 2036.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Implies about fourfold launch-cadence growth, a demand signal for launch providers and range infrastructure.

insights.claim: A third site would ease demand on limited real estate at the Cape and Vandenberg and provide geographic resiliency in case a natural disaster or military attack knocks either offline.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Resiliency framing makes the project a national-security priority rather than just a capacity question.
insights.locator: A third launch site would offload

insights.claim: The government already owns NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia, used for suborbital tests and small and medium launches, and small rockets can fly from Alaska's state-owned Pacific Spaceport Complex.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Existing sites lack heavy-lift capability, which is why a new site is needed.

insights.claim: Asked about leasing a private site such as SpaceX's planned southern Louisiana spaceport, Garrant said public-private partnership, a new federal installation, state land and commercial land are all possibilities, none ruled out.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: SpaceX's Louisiana site could gain a government anchor tenant.
insights.quote: We haven’t made that decision yet, but we’re not discounting any of those options.
